title: Scabies in Far North Queensland, Tropical Australia: Implications for Local Clinical Practice and Public Health Strategies
content: The burden of scabies in Far North Queensland (FNQ), tropical Australia is incompletely defined. We reviewed the results of every skin scraping collected in FNQ’s public health system between 2000 and 2023; 121/4345 (2.8%) were positive, including 19/1071 (1.8%) in the last 5 years of the study; the proportion of tests that were positive for scabies declined over the study period (rs=-0.62, p=0.0001)  Individuals who tested positive for scabies were no more likely to have had a prior diagnosis of ARF or RHD compared to matched controls (1/101 (1%) versus 3/101 (3%); OR (95% CI): 0.32 (0.03–3.20), p=0.33). During a median (IQR) of 14.7 (6.6-20.1) years of follow up, individuals who tested positive for scabies were also no more likely to have a diagnosis of ARF or RHD than matched controls (2/100 (2%) versus 6/98 (6%); hazard ratio (HR) (95% CI): 0.30 (0.06-1.50) p=0.14). We reviewed all 292 individuals diagnosed with scabies in the Cairns Hospital Emergency Department between March 2016 and May 2024. Skin scrapings were performed in 14/292 (4.5%); only 1/14 was positive for scabies. Microbiologically confirmed scabies is uncommon in FNQ and appears to make a limited contribution to the local incidence of ARF and RHD.
